Trying to Conceive

White blood cells in semen: tests, possible causes and treatment

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A semen report showing increased white blood cells can raise worries about infection, sperm health and pregnancy. The useful next step is to confirm what was measured and discuss it with a clinician. Leukocytospermia is a finding with several possible explanations; colour, one number or an online treatment list cannot decide the cause or the best care.

What does a white-cell result mean?

Leukocytes are white blood cells. Increased numbers in semen may be called leukocytospermia or pyospermia. This is a laboratory finding to interpret, not a diagnosis of an STI or permanent infertility. A semen white-cell result is also different from a white-cell count in a blood test.

The WHO laboratory manual uses a consensus threshold of at least 1 million peroxidase-positive cells per millilitre as abnormal. EAU guidance describes leukocytospermia as more than 1 million white cells per millilitre. Ask which cells, method and units your report uses, especially at the boundary; neither wording makes the number a stand-alone fertility verdict.

Confirm which cells were counted

A report of “round cells” does not necessarily mean white cells: immature germ cells can look similar. A laboratory may use a peroxidase stain to identify a major white-cell group. That test does not detect every leukocyte type; a specialist method such as CD45 staining may be used when further identification is needed.

Bring the complete report rather than a photograph of one highlighted number. Ask whether the cells were confirmed, whether the sample needs repeating and how the result fits its volume, sperm concentration, movement and shape. Do not convert cells per microscope field into cells per millilitre yourself or use a home appearance check to confirm the result.

Can white cells damage sperm or prevent pregnancy?

Activated white cells can release reactive oxygen species, which may affect sperm movement and DNA. That biological mechanism does not establish how much damage occurred in a particular person. The reason, location and timing of inflammation and other semen findings matter; a white-cell count does not measure sperm DNA damage.

Research findings about fertility and treatment benefit are inconsistent. Natural conception can remain possible, and an abnormal result does not establish that pregnancy will or will not occur. Both partners’ circumstances need consideration. An isolated white-cell result is not a reason to order every oxidative-stress or sperm-DNA test; specialist guidance differs about selected DNA testing.

Possible explanations need an assessment

Infection or inflammation of the urethra, prostate or other reproductive structures can be involved. Some infections are sexually transmitted, while others are not. Nonbacterial inflammation and chronic pelvic pain also occur. A raised count alone cannot identify a germ, locate the problem or prove that a partner has an infection.

Tell the clinician about urinary problems, recent fever or other illness, previous procedures, injury, medicines and any known inflammatory or immune condition. A varicocele, narrowing or obstruction may warrant attention if the history or examination suggests it, but a list of possible causes cannot diagnose one. There is no reliable universal “under 5% of all men” figure to apply to an individual.

Symptoms and colour are imperfect clues

Some people discover the finding during fertility testing without symptoms. Others have burning urination, pelvic or testicular discomfort, painful ejaculation or discharge. Yellow semen does not prove excess white cells or infection, and usual-looking semen does not exclude either. Fluid appearing outside ejaculation may be urethral discharge and needs its own assessment.

Arrange a clinical appointment for persistent changes, symptoms or an unexplained report. Blood in semen should also be checked. A low sperm count can coexist, but it is a different measurement: current WHO-based reference data use about 16 million sperm per millilitre as the lower reference value, not a universal 15–200 million normal range or a pass/fail fertility test.

What the next appointment may involve

Assessment starts with symptoms, medical and sexual history, fertility goals and an examination. Depending on the findings, the clinician may request urine or STI tests, a semen culture or other targeted investigations. Not everyone needs a scan, hormone panel or invasive test. Ask what each proposed test could change about care.

Follow the laboratory’s collection and delivery instructions and report recent illness, medicines or collection problems. Abnormal semen findings often need confirmation; timing depends on the question. A fertility repeat around three months is common, but major sperm abnormalities may be rechecked sooner. Do not wait for a repeat semen sample if there are symptoms of infection or urgent warning signs.

Sex, condoms and partner care

White cells alone do not prove an STI or justify treating a partner automatically. If there is discharge, a possible exposure or a suspected infection, contact a sexual health service and ask what to do while results are pending. Condoms reduce many STI risks, but do not replace testing or a clinic’s advice to avoid sex.

For diagnosed urethritis or an STI, follow the specific treatment and partner plan. This can mean avoiding sex, including oral sex, until both people have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved; the interval depends on the infection and regimen. Partner notification and repeat STI testing may be needed. A condom is not a substitute for a prescribed abstinence period.

When antibiotics are appropriate

Antibiotics treat susceptible bacterial infections, not white cells themselves. NICE advises against prescribing them solely for seminal leukocytes without an identified infection, because improved pregnancy rates have not been demonstrated. A clinician may nevertheless start treatment before all results return when symptoms and examination establish a clinical infection such as urethritis.

Use only the prescribed medicine and course; do not share antibiotics or extend treatment because a number stays raised. Persistent symptoms need reassessment, including possible reinfection or a different explanation. If antibiotics were prescribed for prostatitis and symptoms worsen or have not improved after 48 hours, seek urgent advice. Improvement in symptoms or a laboratory measurement does not guarantee conception.

Anti-inflammatory medicines are not fertility boosters

Selected inflammatory or pelvic-pain conditions may need symptom treatment, sometimes including an anti-inflammatory medicine. That is different from routinely taking an NSAID to lower semen white cells or increase sperm count. The clinician should identify the purpose, expected benefit and review plan before treatment.

NSAIDs can cause stomach bleeding, kidney problems and interactions with other medicines. Do not combine them or take a prolonged course for a laboratory result without advice. Persistent nonbacterial pelvic pain may need a broader plan, including specialist pain or pelvic-floor care, rather than repeated antibiotics or a promise that one tablet cures the problem.

Antioxidants and vitamins have uncertain benefits

Vitamin C, vitamin E, glutathione and coenzyme Q10 or ubiquinol are often promoted for sperm health. A plausible antioxidant mechanism is not proof that a product treats leukocytospermia or improves the chance of a baby. Treating a documented nutritional deficiency is a separate question from buying a fertility supplement.

In the MOXI randomized trial, a combination supplement did not improve key semen or DNA measurements; the study was too small for a firm live-birth conclusion. It was not a trial specifically of leukocytospermia. Current guidance does not establish a reliable supplement regimen for this finding, and NICE advises against supplements intended to improve sperm DNA integrity. Discuss the actual product and avoid high-dose self-treatment.

Does anyone need surgery?

A white-cell count alone is not an indication for an operation. A clinically detected varicocele with abnormal semen findings and difficulty conceiving may justify a specialist discussion, taking both partners’ fertility into account. A vein seen only on imaging does not automatically require repair.

A proven blockage, significant urinary narrowing or another structural problem has its own treatment pathway. Prostate or urethral surgery is not a general way to “clean” semen, and surgery cannot promise natural conception. Ask which diagnosed problem an intervention would address, its risks and alternatives, and what outcome will be checked afterward.

Support health without blaming yourself

Stopping smoking, reducing heavy alcohol use, manageable exercise and support for a healthy weight can help general reproductive health. Discuss recreational drugs, anabolic steroids and occupational chemical exposure honestly. These steps do not guarantee that white cells disappear, and an abnormal test is not proof that you caused the problem.

A varied diet is preferable to a supplement stack aimed at one number. Do not start testosterone as a fertility aid or stop an essential prescribed medicine yourself. Bring a medicine and supplement list to the appointment, and ask for practical support if changing tobacco, alcohol or drug use is difficult.

Agree a follow-up plan and realistic expectations

Ask when symptoms and test results will be reviewed, whether an infection was actually found and what would change treatment. The goal may be relieving pain, treating an infection, protecting partners or addressing a broader fertility problem. Those goals should not be confused with simply making the white-cell number lower.

Some causes can be treated, but there is no universal cure time or guaranteed pregnancy afterward. Persistent difficulty conceiving deserves assessment of both partners, earlier when there is a known problem rather than waiting for a fixed deadline. Depending on the full findings, choices may include further observation, targeted treatment or assisted reproduction; the white-cell result alone cannot choose among them.

Symptoms that should not wait

Get urgent medical advice for painful urinary or pelvic symptoms with fever or chills, a new testicular lump or swelling, a worrying change in the testicle’s shape or feel, or persistent discomfort. Suspected blood in urine needs urgent assessment even if it is slight or you are unsure. These concerns take priority over a planned fertility test.

Use emergency care for sudden severe testicular pain; testicular pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain; pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest; complete inability to urinate; or severe abdominal pain. Serious illness with sudden confusion, slurred or nonsensical speech, blue/grey/pale/blotchy skin, lips or tongue, a rash that does not fade under pressure, or severe breathing difficulty also needs emergency help. These are alternatives, not a checklist requiring every sign. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring the complete semen report and ask which cells, units and laboratory method were used, whether confirmation is needed and what further tests could change care.

Ask what any proposed treatment is intended to improve: symptoms, an identified infection, partner safety or fertility. Discuss benefits, harms, alternatives and the review date.

Follow the service’s collection, STI and partner instructions; seek help for warning symptoms without waiting for a repeat sample.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize reports, symptom dates, medicines and supplements, treatment instructions and questions for your next appointment. It cannot identify cell types, diagnose an infection, interpret fertility from a semen result, choose antibiotics or assess urgent testicular or urinary symptoms. Recording information must not delay clinical care.

When to seek help

Do not self-treat an isolated white-cell result. Fever or chills with urinary/pelvic symptoms, suspected urine blood or a new testicular change needs urgent advice. Emergency signs include sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea/vomiting or abdominal pain, pain lasting over an hour or at rest, inability to urinate, severe abdominal pain, or serious illness with sudden confusion, abnormal speech, blue/grey/pale/blotchy colour, a non-fading rash or severe breathing difficulty. Not all signs need to occur. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance and do not wait for fertility testing.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Confirm white cells rather than assuming all round cells are leukocytes.
  • An increased count can reflect inflammation without proving an infection or infertility.
  • Treatment should address an identified problem; antibiotics, supplements, NSAIDs and surgery are not automatic.
  • STI advice and partner care depend on the actual diagnosis and treatment plan.
  • Urgent symptoms take priority over fertility testing; agree a follow-up plan for the whole assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Do high white cells definitely damage sperm?

They can contribute to oxidative stress, but the count alone cannot show individual sperm damage or predict fertility. Interpretation needs the confirmed cell type, other semen findings and clinical context. It is not automatically a reason for DNA-fragmentation or oxidative-stress testing.

What can cause leukocytospermia?

Possible explanations include genital or urinary infection and nonbacterial inflammation. Symptoms, history and selected tests distinguish them. A raised result does not identify a specific organism, prove an STI or establish a structural or immune diagnosis.

Is yellow semen the main symptom?

No. Colour does not measure white cells, and the finding may occur without symptoms. Persistent colour change, pain, urinary symptoms or discharge merits assessment. Blood in semen should be checked; suspected blood in urine needs urgent advice.

Is genital infection always the commonest explanation?

An infection needs to be considered, but one laboratory result cannot establish it or rank the cause in an individual. Nonbacterial inflammation exists. Avoid assuming that antibiotics or partner treatment are necessary before assessment.

What does one million cells per millilitre mean?

WHO uses at least one million peroxidase-positive cells per millilitre as an abnormal consensus threshold; EAU describes leukocytospermia as more than one million white cells per millilitre. The assay and cell identification matter. Round cells are not all leukocytes, and neither threshold is a pregnancy prediction.

Will antibiotics, supplements or an anti-inflammatory cure it?

Not automatically. Antibiotics are selected for an infection or a clinically justified presumptive diagnosis; white cells alone do not establish benefit. Supplements and NSAIDs are not proven universal fertility treatments. Treating the cause or improving a result does not guarantee conception.

Can we still try for a pregnancy?

A raised count does not by itself make natural conception impossible. If infection or an STI is suspected, ask the clinic about sex, testing and partner care first; follow any advised abstinence period. Otherwise the full fertility assessment, not one white-cell result, guides the plan.

Which symptoms need emergency care?

Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea/vomiting or abdominal pain, pain lasting over an hour or at rest, inability to urinate or severe abdominal pain needs emergency care. So does serious illness with sudden confusion, abnormal speech, blue/grey/pale/blotchy colour, a non-fading rash or severe breathing difficulty. Do not wait for all signs, a repeat semen test or an app check; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
